newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ban seen on S.Africa direct anchovy fishing in '97.
newsitem.headline: Ban seen on S.Africa direct anchovy fishing in '97.

text.p: Dramatic falls in the level of anchovies along South Africa's coastline may result in a ban on the direct catching of this fish species in 1997, spelling gloom for fishermen and marine firms, industry sources said.

Local anchovy sales, which in bumper years are worth up to 360 million rand, may have to be substituted by expensive imports. The bulk of the catch goes to make fishmeal and oil, and a ban could hit local manufacturers of animal feed hard.

The move follows a recommendation by the country's Sea Fisheries Research Institute to the Minister of Environmental Affairs and Tourism that the Total Allowable Catch (TAC) for anchovies this year be zero.
The institute's Dr Andrew Paine told Reuters on Wednesday the level of anchovy spawners was the lowest since surveys on the fish were started in 1983.
"It is the lowest level in 13 years. That is a dreadfully worrying level for us and we have recommended no fishing for anchovies this year," Paine said.
The Sea Fisheries department said Minister Pallo Jordan was expected to announce the TAC soon, possibly next week. Asked if the TAC could be nil, a spokesman said: "That is a possibility."
The industry has basically accepted a ban as inevitable.

"It could have a devastating effect on the income of fishermen and also the income and profitability of companies," said Andre van Niekerk, the managing director of Marine Products, a subsidiary of Foodcorp Ltd.

But van Niekerk said the drop was not totally unexpected as catches had been small last year when the TAC had fallen to 50,000 tonnes. He said in the past catches as high as 600,000 tonnes had taken place.
"We saw this coming for quite a few years. We have reduced our catching capacity and all our vessels are equipped to catch pilchards," van Niekerk said.
The fishing institute's Paine, however, said that pilchards would not be able to fill the gap left by anchovies. "Pilchards will, at best, be stable this year," he said.

A trader in animal feeds who asked not to be identified told Reuters South Africa would have to import around 110,000 tonnes of fishmeal this year, mainly from Chile, which would be expensive due to the weak rand/dollar exchange rate.

"We will, however, be at least partially compensated by the fact that the usage of fishmeal in animal feed has declined over the years in South Africa. Last year we used about 280,000 tonnes and that will fall to about 140,000 this year," he said.
Paine blamed the decline in anchovies on natural cyclical fluctuations in the fish species, but said fishing obviously speeded up the fall.
The industry looked forward to a better catch next year.

"The good news is that it could swing dramatically as it is a 'one year' fish. If one year the spawning is good then we can have a big TAC again. It is bad at the moment but it can get well quickly," van Niekerk said.
